promptText: A product catalog needs to store nested, self-contained records where each product category has a different set of attributes. Which of the four classic NoSQL families is the natural fit?
options: Document store (e.g. MongoDB)
Wide-column store (e.g. Cassandra)
Key-value store (e.g. Redis)
Graph database (e.g. Neo4j)
explanation: Document stores hold JSON/BSON documents that can nest arbitrary structure per record, which is exactly why they suit flexible, per-category product attributes, whereas the other families are optimized for different shapes (opaque values, dynamic-but-flat columns, or graph traversal).

promptText: What does BSON add on top of plain JSON that makes it useful as MongoDB's on-disk and wire format?
options: Extra typed values like ObjectId, Date and Decimal128, plus a more compact binary encoding
Built-in compression that plain JSON cannot support
A relational schema definition embedded in every document
Native support for SQL joins between collections
explanation: BSON is 'Binary JSON' - it extends JSON with typed values not native to text JSON (ObjectId, Date, Decimal128, 64-bit int) and is faster to traverse and more compact than text JSON, which is why the driver stores and transmits it in that form.

promptText: If you insert a document into MongoDB without supplying an _id, what does MongoDB generate by default?
options: An ObjectId containing a timestamp, a machine/process value and an incrementing counter
A sequential auto-incrementing integer, similar to a relational primary key
A random UUID with no time component at all
A hash computed from the document's field values
explanation: ObjectId is a 12-byte value made of a 4-byte timestamp, a 5-byte random machine/process value, and a 3-byte counter - it is roughly time-ordered but deliberately not sequential like an auto-increment integer.

promptText: In the ESR rule for ordering fields in a MongoDB compound index, what does the letter order (E, S, R) stand for?
options: Equality, Sort, Range
Existence, Scan, Retrieval
Exact, Search, Recall
Entry, Storage, Read
explanation: ESR recommends putting Equality-matched fields first (so the index can seek to the right slice), Sort fields next (so results come back pre-ordered), and Range fields last, since a range condition breaks the ordering guarantee for any fields placed after it.

promptText: According to the embedding-vs-referencing guidance, which scenario is the best candidate for embedding rather than referencing?
options: A one-to-few relationship where the child data is always read together with the parent
An unbounded one-to-many relationship like comments on a post that can go viral
A many-to-many relationship shared across many independent parent documents
Data that needs to be queried and updated independently of its parent
explanation: Embedding is best when data is read together and the relationship is one-to-few with no independent life of its own; unbounded or independently-queried data should be referenced instead, partly because of the hard 16MB document size limit.

promptText: During an actual network partition, what does the CAP theorem say a distributed database must choose between?
options: Consistency or Availability
Consistency or Durability
Availability or Durability
Atomicity or Isolation
explanation: CAP states that when a partition occurs, a system can only guarantee Consistency or Availability, not both - partition tolerance itself is not optional in a distributed system, so the real choice only arises while the partition is happening.

promptText: Why is it deliberately useful that MongoDB's ObjectId is randomized rather than a simple sequential counter?
options: A sequential key would make every new insert route to the same shard, creating a hot shard, whereas randomness spreads writes across shards
Sequential keys are not permitted at all by the BSON specification
Random values compress better on disk than sequential integers
It allows _id values to be reused safely after a document is deleted
explanation: A monotonically increasing key always has the current highest value routed to the same shard, creating a permanent write hotspot; ObjectId's random component avoids this exact problem, which is the same underlying issue as the monotonic shard-key pitfall at the collection-sharding level.

promptText: Why must range-filtered fields (like $gt or $lt) come after equality and sort fields in a compound index, rather than before them?
options: Once the index starts ranging over a field, the ordering guarantee for any fields listed after it is lost
MongoDB's query language forbids placing a range operator anywhere except last in a filter document
Range fields must always be the largest data type in the index
Placing a range field early would prevent the index from being created at all
explanation: Equality fields let MongoDB seek directly to a slice, and sort fields let it return pre-ordered results, but a range scan over a field destroys any preserved ordering for subsequent fields - so ranges must go last or the planner falls back to an expensive in-memory sort.

promptText: In a Cassandra table definition, what is the distinct job of the clustering key compared to the partition key?
options: The clustering key determines the sort order of rows within a partition, while the partition key determines which node(s) hold the data
The clustering key determines which node holds the data, while the partition key determines row order on disk
Both keys perform the same job and are used interchangeably for load balancing
The clustering key is used only for secondary indexing, unrelated to physical storage
explanation: The partition key is hashed to a token that decides physical placement across the cluster, while the clustering key only controls how rows are ordered on disk within that one partition - conflating the two is a common mistake since only the partition key affects distribution.

promptText: Why are writes in Cassandra so cheap compared to a typical read-modify-write on a relational engine?
options: Writes are sequential appends to a commit log and an in-memory memtable, with no read-before-write or in-place update
Cassandra buffers all writes in application memory and never persists them to disk
Cassandra skips durability guarantees entirely to maximize write throughput
Every write is automatically batched with the next 100 writes before being applied
explanation: Cassandra's LSM-tree storage engine appends writes to a commit log and a memtable with no random disk seek or read-before-write, which is what makes sustained write throughput so high - the trade-off shows up later on the read side as read/compaction amplification.

promptText: A query projects only the fields present in the index used to satisfy it, and explain() shows totalDocsExamined: 0. What does this indicate, and what is the most common reason a query that should be covered ends up not being?
options: It is a covered query answered entirely from the index; forgetting to explicitly exclude _id in the projection usually breaks it
It means the query used a COLLSCAN; adding any index fixes it
It means the query is covered only if it also uses $lookup; aggregation always defeats coverage
It indicates the write concern was set to majority; read preference settings usually break it
explanation: A covered query is answered entirely from the index with no document fetch, shown by totalDocsExamined: 0 and no FETCH stage - but _id is always indexed on its own and is included by default, so forgetting to exclude it from the projection forces an unnecessary document fetch.

promptText: What is the main caveat that keeps Redis from being treated as a general-purpose primary database for every workload, even though it supports persistence and replication?
options: The data set needs to fit comfortably in RAM, and its durability model is weaker than a WAL-backed disk store
Redis cannot replicate data across multiple nodes under any configuration
Redis only supports plain string values and cannot model structured records
Redis requires a relational schema to be defined before any writes are accepted
explanation: Redis is a legitimate primary store for leaderboards, rate limiters, and session state, but because it is RAM-resident and its AOF fsync trade-offs are weaker than a disk-backed WAL, workloads needing rich ad-hoc queries or the strongest durability (like financial ledgers) still belong in an ACID store.

promptText: A Cassandra keyspace has replication factor RF=3. For one query the application uses write concern W=1 and, separately for a different read, consistency level R=1. Why does this combination NOT guarantee the read observes the most recent write, whereas QUORUM writes and QUORUM reads (W=2, R=2) would?
options: Strong consistency requires R + W > RF; 1 + 1 = 2 is not greater than 3, so the read and write sets are not guaranteed to overlap on an up-to-date replica
W=1 and R=1 are invalid consistency levels in Cassandra and would be rejected outright
Replication factor only affects availability, never consistency guarantees
Quorum reads always return stale data regardless of the write concern used
explanation: The classic guarantee is R + W > RF: with RF=3, QUORUM+QUORUM gives 2+2=4 > 3 so the read and write sets must share at least one up-to-date replica, but W=1 with R=1 gives only 2, which is not greater than RF=3, so a stale replica can be the one read from.

promptText: A sharded MongoDB collection uses an ever-increasing insertion timestamp as its shard key, and the team notices one shard taking almost all write load. What is happening, and what is a standard mitigation?
options: Every new insert has the current highest key value, which always routes to the same shard, creating a permanent hot shard; hashing the shard key (or combining it with a coarse, evenly-distributed bucket) spreads writes evenly
The shard key has too many distinct values, so MongoDB is unable to build a routing table at all
This is expected and unrelated to shard key choice; adding more replica set members fixes it
The mongos router is misconfigured and needs to be restarted to rebalance chunks
explanation: A monotonically increasing shard key always places new writes at the current top of the range, which lives on one shard, defeating the purpose of sharding; hashing the key trades away range-query locality in exchange for evenly distributed writes, or a compound key can combine a bucket with the monotonic field.

promptText: A team needs to decrement inventory in one collection while creating an order document in another, atomically, because a half-done update would corrupt business state. What is the recommended senior approach to this requirement?
options: First check whether the invariant-holding fields can be embedded into a single document to get single-document atomicity for free; reach for a multi-document transaction only if that redesign genuinely isn't possible
Always use a multi-document transaction as the default tool for any operation touching more than one document
Avoid transactions entirely and rely on eventual consistency to reconcile inventory and orders over time
Switch the entire inventory and order system to Cassandra, since MongoDB cannot guarantee cross-collection atomicity
explanation: Multi-document transactions take locks across documents/collections, hold a snapshot, and add real cross-shard coordination overhead if collections span shards - so the strongest answer treats them as an escape hatch used only when the invariant truly cannot be pushed into a single document via schema redesign, not as the default pattern.
